title: PropertyReady: selling and renting residential property in Western Australia
notes: First sourced rules for SellReady and RentReady in Western Australia. Built from Consumer Protection (consumerprotection.wa.gov.au, formerly at commerce.wa.gov.au), Building and Energy (wa.gov.au) and Landgate pages read on 2026-10-12. Every reference is UNVERIFIED and carries a summary, not the source's wording: staff must capture each source, replace the extract with the exact text and verify it. The Residential Tenancies Act 1987, Residential Tenancies Regulations 1989, Strata Titles Act 1985, Building Regulations 2012, Electricity Regulations and Duties Act 2008 were not read directly.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Stage two of the WA rental reforms started on 29 July 2024. Rent can only be increased once every 12 months (up from every 6 months). Tenants can keep pets in most cases but must ask first; a landlord can refuse only where a law or by-law prevents it or with a good reason accepted by the Commissioner for Consumer Protection, and can set reasonable conditions. Tenants can make minor modifications (for example hanging pictures or child safety locks) with permission, which can be refused only on limited grounds or with the Commissioner's approval, and must restore the premises at the end unless the landlord agrees otherwise. Rent bidding was banned earlier, in May 2024. A Commissioner determination process decides these disputes, and was extended to bond releases from early 2025.
references.interpretation: Applies to every residential tenancy in WA. The Residential Tenancies Act 1987 and the amending Act were not read directly. Captured on 2026-10-12 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.section: How much can be charged; pet bonds; releasing the bond
references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] A landlord can take up to 4 weeks' rent as a bond, unless the rent is over $1,200 a week. A pet bond of up to $350 can be taken for fumigation and pet-related damage. Existing pet bonds can only be raised to the new amount at the next rent increase or when another pet is approved. A receipt must be given straight away. Bonds Administration releases the bond on a bond release form signed by all tenants and landlords, a Commissioner's decision, or a court or tribunal order.
references.interpretation: Applies to every residential tenancy bond in WA. Captured on 2026-10-12 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.section: Who lodges and when; how to lodge
references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] The landlord must lodge the bond with Bonds Administration as soon as possible and no later than 14 days after the tenant pays it. The lodgement lists every tenant on the agreement, the amount, any pet bond and tenant contact details. Agents and property managers must use BondsOnline. Private landlords can use BondsOnline or the paper bond lodgement form if eligible. Bonds Administration sends a record of payment to all parties; call 1300 30 40 54 if none arrives within a month.
references.interpretation: Applies whenever a bond is taken for a WA residential tenancy. Captured on 2026-10-12 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] The WA notice of termination is the landlord's notice of termination for reasons other than unpaid rent, and only one ground can be given. Grounds include: a breach not remedied (at least 7 days, after a breach notice given 14 days earlier); a contract of sale requiring vacant possession (at least 30 days, not during a fixed term); without grounds (at least 60 days, not during a fixed term); and ending a fixed-term agreement on its expiry date (at least 30 days).
references.interpretation: The form read was the version published in July 2025 and still includes ending a periodic tenancy without grounds on 60 days' notice, so no-grounds termination of periodic tenancies has not been removed in WA. Captured on 2026-10-12 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] The landlord must give the tenant 2 copies of the WA property condition report within 7 days of the tenant moving in. The tenant returns one completed copy within 7 days of receiving it. At the end, the landlord gives the tenant a copy of the outgoing report within 14 days of the tenant moving out.
references.interpretation: Applies to every WA residential tenancy. Captured on 2026-10-12 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Rent can be increased no more than once every 12 months under periodic and fixed-term agreements. The tenant must get at least 60 days' notice on the WA rent increase notice. In a fixed-term agreement the increase or how it is worked out must be written in the agreement. Long fixed-term agreements signed before 29 July 2024 keep their written-in increases until the end of the tenancy.
references.interpretation: Applies to every WA residential tenancy. Captured on 2026-10-12 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Under the Residential Tenancies Regulations 1989, the main entry door must be key-lockable with a deadlock or an AS 5039-2008 security screen door; other external doors need a deadlock, a patio bolt lock or a compliant security screen door; windows need a lock that stops them being opened from outside (unless not easily reached or fitted with a compliant screen); and there must be an electric light at or near the main entry that can be switched on from inside. Agricultural, rural and heritage-listed homes are exempt but must still be reasonably secure. Landlords can't change locks without the tenant's consent except in limited cases.
references.interpretation: Applies to WA rentals that are not agricultural, rural or heritage listed. A wider set of minimum standards (for example structural, plumbing) was not found on the page read. Captured on 2026-10-12 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] A dwelling must have compliant smoke alarms before ownership is transferred, and before it is rented or hired. Alarms must be permanently connected to mains power, unless there is no hidden space for wiring and no other suitable place, in which case a 10-year non-removable battery alarm can be used. Alarms must be no more than 10 years old and not past their expiry date, and interconnected where there is more than one (unless the building permit was applied for before 1 May 2015). Only a licensed electrical contractor can connect mains alarms. A buyer who intends to demolish within 6 months can give the seller a statutory declaration instead. Local governments enforce the rules under the Building Act 2011 and Building Regulations 2012.
references.interpretation: Applies to every WA dwelling being sold, rented or hired. Captured on 2026-10-12 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Before the land title is transferred on sale, at least two RCDs (safety switches) must protect all power point and lighting circuits; if not, the seller must have a licensed electrical contractor install them. Landlords must make sure RCDs are installed in the switchboard of a rental home. These requirements come from the Electricity Regulations.

The landlord must keep smoke alarms compliant, mains powered and under 10 years old, and use licensed electrical contractors for electrical repairs. references.section: Pre-contract disclosure; notifiable variations; avoiding the contract
references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Before contract the seller gives the scheme notice, scheme plan, by-laws, schedule of unit entitlements, any strata lease, the latest AGM and later EGM minutes, the latest statement of accounts, any termination proposal, estimated levies for 12 months and any money owed to the strata company, plus details of the lot and its unit entitlement. Notifiable variations must be notified within 10 working days. If the information was not given, the buyer may be able to avoid the contract before settlement, in some cases only if materially prejudiced. The seller or buyer can ask the strata company for information in writing and inspect records for a $1 fee.
references.interpretation: Applies to strata lot sales in WA. The fact sheet does not name the prescribed disclosure form. references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Written rental agreements must use the WA residential tenancy agreement; you can't write your own. Before the tenant moves in, the landlord gives a copy of the signed agreement within 14 days of signing, the WA information for tenant sheet (a separate sheet applies to verbal agreements), 2 copies of the property condition report within 7 days, a copy of any strata or community title by-laws, a completed bond lodgement form for the tenant to sign, and keys. Part B of the agreement can't be changed and Part C terms can't remove rights under tenancy or consumer laws.
references.interpretation: Applies to every WA residential tenancy. Captured on 2026-10-12 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.section: Offer and acceptance; General Conditions; special conditions
references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] An offer to buy a WA property is usually made on the Offer and Acceptance form together with the Joint Form of General Conditions for the Sale of Land, and a printed copy of the General Conditions should be given to both seller and buyer. rule_sets.title: Western Australia: selling a property
rule_sets.description: The offer and acceptance and Joint Form of General Conditions, settlement agents, strata disclosure, smoke alarms and RCDs before transfer, pool barriers, transfer duty and selling with a tenant, from Consumer Protection, Building and Energy, Landgate and RevenueWA guidance.
limitations: Built from Consumer Protection, Building and Energy, Landgate and RevenueWA web pages, not from the Sale of Land Act 1970, Strata Titles Act 1985, Building Regulations 2012 or Electricity Regulations.
Doesn't prepare the offer and acceptance or decide which special conditions you need; your agent and settlement agent do that.

rules.title: Contract of sale and disclosure in WA
rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified.

outcomes.title: Sell on a written offer and acceptance, and disclose what you know
outcomes.detail: WA has no general vendor disclosure statement like other states. Most homes are sold on a written offer and acceptance that adopts the Joint Form of General Conditions for the Sale of Land, usually prepared by your real estate agent. Settlement is normally handled by a licensed settlement agent or a lawyer. Tell your agent and settlement agent about anything that affects the property, such as unapproved building work, strata matters, a tenancy or a pool, so it is dealt with in the contract. Use the 'Before you sell' checklist to get ready.

outcomes.title: Choose a licensed settlement agent or a lawyer
outcomes.detail: In WA, settlement (transferring the title, adjusting rates and paying out any mortgage) is done by a licensed settlement agent or a lawyer. Choose one before you accept an offer so they can check the contract conditions and dates. You can check a settlement agent's licence with Consumer Protection.

rules.title: Strata seller disclosure
rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified.

outcomes.title: Give the buyer the strata disclosure before they sign
outcomes.detail: If you are selling a strata lot, the Strata Titles Act 1985 requires you to give the buyer set information before they sign: the scheme notice, plan, by-laws and unit entitlements, any strata lease, the latest AGM and later EGM minutes, the latest accounts, any termination proposal, 12 months of estimated levies and any money you owe the strata company. Use the WA strata seller disclosure statement. Ask your strata manager for the records early. If you don't disclose, the buyer may be able to get out of the contract before settlement. After signing, tell the buyer in writing about any notifiable variation within 10 working days.

outcomes.detail: Strata lots (including many villas and townhouses, and survey-strata lots) carry extra disclosure duties when sold. Check your certificate of title, or ask Landgate or your settlement agent, whether the property is in a strata scheme.

rules.title: Smoke alarms before transfer
rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified.

outcomes.title: Install compliant smoke alarms before ownership transfers
outcomes.detail: Before a WA home is transferred to the buyer, it must have smoke alarms that are permanently connected to mains power (a 10-year sealed battery alarm only where there is no space for wiring), no more than 10 years old, and interconnected if there is more than one and the building permit was applied for after 1 May 2015. Only a licensed electrical contractor can install mains alarms. Book the work well before settlement. If the buyer plans to demolish within 6 months, they can give you a statutory declaration instead.

payload.task: Have smoke alarms checked and upgraded before settlement

rules.title: Two RCDs before transfer
rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified.

outcomes.title: Make sure at least two RCDs protect all power and lighting circuits
outcomes.detail: Before the title is transferred, a WA home must have at least two RCDs (safety switches) protecting all power point and lighting circuits. Look at your switchboard; if there are fewer than two RCDs or some circuits aren't covered, have a licensed electrical contractor install them before settlement and keep the invoice for your settlement agent.

payload.task: Check the switchboard has at least two RCDs covering all circuits

rules.title: Pool barrier
rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified.

outcomes.title: Make sure the pool barrier complies before you list
outcomes.detail: Every private pool, spa or portable pool deeper than 30cm in WA needs a compliant safety barrier, and your local government inspects it at least every four years. WA has no pool certificate for sale, but the buyer or their agent may ask when it was last inspected. Check gates self-close and latch, nothing climbable is near the fence, and fix any defects from the last council inspection. Ask your council for the last inspection result.

payload.task: Check the pool barrier and get the last council inspection result

rules.title: Selling with a tenant
rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified.

outcomes.title: Plan the sale around the tenancy
outcomes.detail: A tenant with a fixed-term agreement can stay until it ends, and you can't end a fixed term early because you are selling. If the tenancy is periodic and the contract requires vacant possession, you can give the tenant at least 30 days' notice on the WA notice of termination after the contract is signed. To end a fixed term on its expiry date you must give at least 30 days' notice. Tell your agent so the offer says whether the buyer takes the property with the tenant.

payload.task: Decide whether to sell with vacant possession or with the tenant

rules.title: Managing the tenancy until settlement
rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified.

outcomes.title: Keep the tenancy on track until settlement with RentReady
outcomes.detail: Your tenant stays through the sale, so WA tenancy rules still apply until the buyer takes over: entry notices, repairs, rent and the bond. RentReady keeps that checklist for you.

rules.title: Transfer duty and settlement costs
rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified.

outcomes.title: The buyer pays transfer duty; your settlement agent handles the transfer
outcomes.detail: In WA the buyer pays transfer duty to RevenueWA, usually through their settlement agent. As the seller you mainly pay your agent's commission, settlement agent fees and any mortgage discharge costs; council rates and water charges are adjusted at settlement. Ask your settlement agent for an estimate of your costs.

payload.task: Get a settlement cost estimate from your settlement agent

outcomes.title: Use the WA residential tenancy agreement and give the tenant the start-up documents
outcomes.detail: A written WA tenancy must use the WA residential tenancy agreement; you can't write your own. Give the tenant a copy within 14 days of signing, plus the WA information for tenant sheet, any strata by-laws, a completed WA bond lodgement form to sign, and keys. outcomes.title: Lodge the bond with Bonds Administration within 14 days
outcomes.detail: You can't keep a WA bond yourself. Lodge it with Bonds Administration (Consumer Protection) no later than 14 days after the tenant pays, using BondsOnline or, for private landlords who qualify, the WA bond lodgement form. Give the tenant a receipt straight away. If you're not sure it was lodged, call Bonds Administration on 1300 30 40 54 or ask your property manager.

outcomes.title: Use the WA notice of termination and the right notice period
outcomes.detail: To end a WA tenancy for reasons other than unpaid rent, use the WA notice of termination. A periodic tenancy can still be ended without grounds, with at least 60 days' notice, or with 30 days' notice after a sale contract that needs vacant possession. outcomes.detail: As a self-managing WA landlord you prepare the agreement and condition reports, lodge the bond within 14 days, give notices on the right forms and keep smoke alarms, RCDs and locks compliant.
